segments.say: We've travelled a long way tonight, from a night in Queens in 1964, to a doorway on a campus, to a jogger in a football shirt, to a kidney donor's brain scan. Let's finish by pulling the threads together into something you can use.

If one message runs through all of this research, it's that whether a person helps depends enormously on the situation. Not on whether they are good or bad, but on whether they noticed, whether they were hurrying, whether others were watching, whether they felt it was their place, and whether they knew what to do.

show.sub: Helping is a situation as well as a trait

segments.say: Remember where we began. Thirty-eight silent witnesses turned out to be a story, and not a fact. CCTV footage showed that in nine of ten public conflicts, somebody stepped in. The truth about human beings is more hopeful than the myth, and more demanding.

show.title: The map of this video
items: The silent crowd was partly a myth
Ambiguity and diffusion can freeze us
Hurry narrows what we notice
Mood and empathy raise the chance of helping
Children are ready to help early
Groups and norms shape who we help
Training and plans make action more likely
Help works best when it respects the receiver

segments.say: Here is a short toolkit, drawn from the research. It's not a set of rules, but a handful of habits that psychologists have found to matter.
These seven habits come from different studies, but they fit together. The first three are about the moment of need. The next two are about preparation. The last two are about the long run.

show.title: Seven habits of a helper
items: Slow down enough to notice
Ask out loud when you are unsure
Name a specific person when you need help
Widen your sense of us
Make a plan in advance
Ask before you help
Look after yourself so you can last

segments.say: Looking across the studies, no single habit is magic, and none of the findings is without its caveats. Some of the classic results have been revised, some rest on small samples, and many were done in one country. The fair summary is that these are well-supported tendencies, to be used with judgement.

We do not know exactly how much of helping is inborn and how much is learned. We do not know how well laboratory results carry into real life. And we do not know whether any of these habits can transform a person who has little inclination to help. What we know is that most people want to be helpful, and that small changes make it easier.

Now let's slow down. If you're listening at the end of the day, this is a good moment to let go of the work of understanding, and simply let the ideas settle. You've heard a lot of studies. You don't need to remember any of them.

Six terms to take away. Prosocial behaviour is acting to benefit others. Diffusion of responsibility is the feeling that someone else will deal with it. Pluralistic ignorance is when everyone looks calm and so no one acts. Empathic concern is warm care for another. Common ingroup identity is a shared, larger we. And an implementation intention is an if-then plan.

show.title: Words to keep from the whole video
items: Prosocial behaviour
Diffusion of responsibility
Pluralistic ignorance
Empathic concern
Common ingroup identity
Implementation intention

segments.say: If you take only five things, take these. Most people help when the need is clear. Name one person to break the silence. Leave a little slack in your day. Ask before you help. And rest, so you can keep on caring. Picture this scene: you're walking home. It's evening, the light is low, and you notice a person standing at a bus stop looking at a phone with a worried face. You're not in a hurry tonight. You say, hi, are you all right? She says, my battery died, and I don't know when the bus comes. You tell her the times. She smiles. You both walk on. It took thirty seconds, and it is exactly what all of this research is about.

show.title: Five things to take from this video
items: Most people help when need is clear
Name one person to break the silence
Leave a little slack in your day
Ask before you help
Rest, so that you can keep caring

segments.say: A final pause before we rest. What did you notice about yourself as you listened? Perhaps you recognised a moment when you hesitated, or a time when someone helped you at just the right moment. Perhaps you felt a little guilty, and perhaps relieved. Which of the seven habits would you like to try first? You don't need to try them all. One is plenty. And who would you like to tell about it? Ideas become habits more easily when they are shared. Finally, think of something you could do tomorrow in thirty seconds, such as asking someone whether they are all right, thanking a person who helped you, or replying to a message you have been postponing. That is the whole of it. The research does not ask us to be heroes. It asks us to notice, to ask, and to act in small ways, again and again.

show.title: Pause and reflect
items: What did I notice about myself in this video?
Which habit would I try first?
Who would I like to tell about it?
What could I do tomorrow, in thirty seconds?

segments.say: A quiet street at night, with lit windows along it. Behind each window, someone is probably having a hard day, or a good one. Most of the helping in the world happens in streets like this, unseen and unrecorded, and it is easy to begin. As the night goes quiet, remember that none of this needs to be done perfectly. A question, a plan, a pause for rest: these are small things, and they are what the whole body of research comes down to.

There is no minimum size for kindness. A question, a held door, a message answered, a seat given up: each is exactly the kind of act that the research is about. And each, as we have seen, makes the next one more likely.

So what did we learn? That the famous story of silent witnesses was largely a myth. That whether we help depends on the situation more than we thought. That we can notice, ask, plan and widen our circles. And that helping well includes respecting others and looking after ourselves.

show.sub: What the whole video taught us

segments.say: Thank you for listening to the end. If this video helped, consider sharing it with someone who might enjoy it, and subscribing for more calm, sourced psychology. Sleep well, and be kind to yourself tonight.
